analysis.one_liner: Makes willful robocalling a crime, with up to three years in prison for repeat or large-scale violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, with no cosponsors, until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly break the existing ban on automated telemarketing calls and texts — up to one year in prison, and up to three years for repeat offenders, for robocall operations running at massive scale, for calls tied to other felonies, or for calls causing $5,000 or more in losses in a year. It would also double the fine for deliberately faking caller ID to $20,000. Instead of just civil fines after the fact, law enforcement could prosecute the people running large illegal robocall operations.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone. Illegal robocalls are among the most common consumer complaints, and many are outright fraud attempts — fake warranty renewals, Social Security scams, phony debt collection. Criminal penalties and higher fake-caller-ID fines give prosecutors and phone carriers stronger tools to go after the operators behind these campaigns, and the threat of jail adds deterrence that civil fines on shell companies often lack.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone annoyed or defrauded by robocalls

how_it_helps.text: Adds criminal penalties — up to one year in prison — for willfully and knowingly violating the prohibition on automated telemarketing calls and messages [S2][S3].

Adds an aggravated offense carrying up to three years in prison for repeat offenders, callers initiating huge volumes (100,000 calls in a day, a million in a month, 10 million in a year), calls made to further a felony, or calls causing $5,000 or more in combined losses in a year [S2][S3].

Doubles the maximum fine for intentionally transmitting misleading or inaccurate caller identification information from $10,000 to $20,000, targeting spoofing that makes scam calls look local or official [S2][S3].
Criminal liability attaches only to willful and knowing violations, so the penalties aim at illegal robocall operations rather than legitimate telemarketing or ordinary dialing mistakes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The people and companies running large illegal robocall and spoofing operations, who would face prison time and larger fines instead of civil penalties. Legitimate telemarketers who call carefully within the rules would bear little new risk, though any business that calls consumers now faces criminal exposure if it knowingly crosses the line.
analysis.who_pays_short: Illegal robocall operators and call spoofers

drawbacks.text: Criminalizing regulatory violations raises the stakes for any telemarketer or business that calls consumers; a company that knowingly runs afoul of the automated-call rules could face prosecution rather than just fines, a line some argue should stay civil [S2][S3].
The bill adds penalties but creates no new enforcement funding, staffing, or call-blocking requirements, so its practical effect depends entirely on prosecutors choosing to bring cases [S2].
Big robocall operations are often run through hard-to-reach shell companies and overseas callers, so prison terms may deter some operators without stopping the calls themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: stronger deterrence against a nuisance and fraud problem that touches nearly every household, at essentially no cost to taxpayers or to people who follow the law. The main cost is the risk of over-criminalizing conduct by businesses that call consumers, though the willful-and-knowing standard and the volume thresholds are drawn to target large-scale illegal operations. The bigger weakness is that the bill adds no enforcement capacity of its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, passed along to a subcommittee, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Susie Lee introduced the bill on July 17, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, where it stayed [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever acted on it, it attracted no cosponsors, and it never reached the House floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The operators of large illegal robocall and caller-ID spoofing campaigns are better off, because the criminal penalties that would have exposed them to prison time never became law. Phone users remain stuck with the same civil-penalty regime that has not stopped the calls.

for.name: Rep. Susie Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add criminal penalties for willful robocall violations and higher fines for fake caller ID.

sides.party_line_note: No one opposed the bill on the record — it simply drew no cosponsors and no committee action from either party, and never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill turns willful violations of the automated-call ban into a crime, with prison terms of up to three years for large-scale or repeat operations, and doubles the fake-caller-ID fine. Its death leaves these operators facing only the existing civil fines.

Carriers profit from carrying robocall traffic, and criminal liability that reaches anyone who 'initiates' a call — including transmitting one — would give them a stronger incentive to police the traffic on their networks. The bill's death keeps that pressure off.
